metadata.title: What the Tools Cannot Do
metadata.topic: Three constitutive limits of AI — meaning (symbol grounding), intentionality (original vs derived), and the data-world gap (distribution shift) — plus the override that has to be real (moral crumple zones, Challenger) and calibration as practice
metadata.purpose: deep-explainer episode 4 — the third leg of the set (epistemology, fluency, limits)
metadata.audience: practitioners and makers following the channel's Claude workflows
metadata.source: computational-skepticism-for-ai (source doc: The Limits of AI — Research Deepening, pasted 2026-07-21; on disk as SOURCE.md)
metadata.notes: Challenger beats use NASA public-domain imagery (tier 2, sidecar) and the PRECISE Rogers Commission attribution: Mason to Lund, 'take off your engineering hat and put on your management hat' — never the looser NASA-to-Boisjoly version. No depiction of the accident itself — pre-launch imagery only. Named scholars (Harnad, Searle, Dennett, Elish, Guo) attributed, no portraits.

beats.narration_text: Jambo — this is Liam, in for Bear. Today's ask is the claim that's easy to state and hard to sit with: some limits on AI aren't engineering problems waiting on scale. They're constitutive — part of what these systems are. A system that manipulates symbols without a model of their referents doesn't get one by manipulating more symbols, faster.

props.topic: Three constitutive limits of AI — meaning (symbol grounding), intentionality (original vs derived), and the data-world gap (distribution shift) — plus the override that has to be real (moral crumple zones, Challenger) and calibration as practice

props.command: Which limits of AI systems are permanent — and what does an honest deployment do about them?
output: Three limits: meaning, intentionality, the data-world gap.
None of them are waiting on a bigger model.
The honest move is naming them — and making the override real.

beats.narration_text: Act one. Three limits — and why the reflex objection, 'but it'll improve,' doesn't touch any of them.

Meaning. Intentionality. The gap between data and world. The claim isn't that these are hard — they're constitutive: properties of what the system is, not defects in its size. Watch the scale lever pull — more data, more compute — and watch what doesn't move.
beats.new_visual_element: Three limits vs the scale lever

show.event: three limit chips draw: MEANING · ABOUTNESS · DATA≠WORLD
a SCALE lever cranks; parameter/data counters spin wildly
the three chips do not move a pixel — terracotta ring around their stillness

props.note: the lever spins; the chips hold

beats.narration_text: Act two. Meaning — or in cognitive science's precise vocabulary, the symbol grounding problem.

show.event: act card 'Meaning'

beats.narration_text: Stevan Harnad, nineteen ninety, posed it with a dictionary. Every word in here is defined using other words in the same book. Perfectly consistent. Completely sealed.
beats.new_visual_element: VOX run R1 (1/2): the dictionary, tight
beats.prompt: Tier 1. Macro of an open dictionary page, dense entries, one plate serves B04+B05. See SHOPPING.md.

show.event: tight on the entries; slow drift along a definition
serif label: 'Harnad, 1990 — the symbol grounding problem'

beats.narration_text: Hand it to a reader who knows no language at all, and they get nothing — no matter how large the dictionary. Symbols defined by symbols never bootstrap their own connection to the world. Scale the book a millionfold. The seal holds.
beats.new_visual_element: VOX run R1 (2/2): the sealed book revealed

show.event: camera eases OUT from the handoff — the whole massive volume, closed world
serif label: 'the seal holds'; terracotta underline

beats.narration_text: That's the clinical case in one picture: outputs correctly related to every symbol in the corpus — whether they relate to this patient's actual body is a question the symbol-web can't answer from inside. Bender and Koller made it formal: text prediction trains on form. Form alone doesn't yield meaning.

show.event: a dense node-web of symbols, edges only to each other; it pulses fluently
outside the web, a patient-mark; every attempted edge from web to patient stops at a boundary ring
'form ≠ meaning — Bender & Koller' citation chip, small

production_viz.label: symbols all the way down
production_viz.mechanic: closed graph; edges cannot cross the boundary to the referent

beats.narration_text: Now the distinction that catches the overclaiming: document grounding versus world grounding. A pipeline citing a real clinical guideline is grounded in the document sense. Whether that guideline still describes this patient, right now — that's world grounding, and the citation doesn't answer it. In fast settings, one impersonates the other.

show.event: a claim chip anchors DOWN to a document chip — clean citation link, check
the document's link to THE WORLD flickers — the world-state drifts ahead of the corpus timestamp
'a citation is not a current world' — terracotta

beats.narration_text: The engineering discipline that falls out: never let fluency-confidence stand in for grounding-confidence. We asked Claude for the flag.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk micro-beat, spark line 'Fluent is not grounded.'

props.command: Write a check that separates document grounding from world grounding: flag when the referent isn't resolved to a real record, and when that record may be stale relative to the actual case.

beats.narration_text: Two separate checks. Entity resolution — is the claim tied to a real record? That's document grounding. Freshness — is the record still an accurate description of the case? That's the world check the citation misses. And even both passing ends in the same line: still requires human semantic sign-off.

show.event: Onda code-block: flag_ungrounded_output() — real file, lines reveal with the voice
the final PROCEED line highlights on 'human semantic sign-off'

beats.narration_text: Act three. Intentionality — and Searle's own name for the distinction this limit rides on.

show.event: act card 'Aboutness'

beats.narration_text: Original intentionality: when you think about your kettle, the aboutness is intrinsic to the thought. Derived intentionality is borrowed — symbols stand for things because minds lend them the standing. Searle's claim, applied: a system's outputs carry derived aboutness at best — on loan from whoever built it and whoever's reading it.
beats.new_visual_element: Original v. derived — the borrowed arrow

show.event: a mind-mark aims a solid arrow at a kettle-mark — arrow originates INSIDE the mind
a system-mark's arrow at the kettle draws DASHED — its tail visibly anchored back in two human marks (builder, reader)
'on loan' — terracotta label on the dashed tail

production_viz.label: original v. derived
production_viz.mechanic: solid intrinsic arrow vs dashed arrow anchored in human marks

beats.narration_text: There's a test a reviewer can actually run. Remove the human reader and operator entirely — what intentional content survives? If the honest answer is none beyond the patterns humans read in, the aboutness was derived all the way down — and the product should stop being sold as if it understands.
beats.prompt: Tier 1. An empty chair facing a glowing screen in a dark room — the reader removed. See SHOPPING.md.

show.event: treated plate; slow push past the empty chair toward the glowing screen
serif label: 'remove the reader — what remains?'

beats.narration_text: Honest caveat — the debate isn't closed. Dennett rejects the whole framework: no intrinsic aboutness anywhere, just attributions that earn their keep by predicting behavior. Fine. That lowers the bar; it doesn't grant understanding. Either way the deployment question sharpens: is predictive usefulness enough here, or is someone selling understanding?
beats.new_visual_element: The Dennett caveat — the bar moves, the claim doesn't

show.event: two bars: 'original aboutness' high, 'predictive usefulness' lower; Dennett's move strikes the high bar
the product-claim chip still hovers ABOVE the lower bar on 'selling understanding' — flagged terracotta

props.note: Boden's caution logged: don't overload intentionality arguments

beats.narration_text: Act four. The most measurable limit of the three — the data is always less than the world.

show.event: act card 'The Data-World Gap'

beats.narration_text: The technical vocabulary is mature: distributional shift, three flavors. Covariate shift — the inputs change. Label shift — the outcomes change. Concept drift — the relationship between them changes. Three ways the world walks away from the training data, all wearing the same disguise: a model that keeps answering.

show.event: a training-cloud and a world-cloud overlap; three animated separations play in turn: inputs slide, outcome mix re-weights, the mapping arrow bends
in all three, the model's answer-ticker keeps ticking — unchanged

beats.narration_text: And it's measured, not intuited. The WILDS benchmark was built from real deployment shifts — across hospitals, camera traps, time, geography — and its sobering result: performance degrades materially out-of-distribution, and the gap survives the robustness methods aimed at closing it. Same model, different hospital, different truth.
beats.prompt: Tier 1. Hospital corridor, institutional light, one imaging monitor glowing at a nurses' station. See SHOPPING.md.

show.event: treated plate; slow push down the corridor
serif label: 'same model, different hospital' (WILDS, cited)

beats.narration_text: The trap inside the trap: the model's own confidence is not a safeguard. Guo and colleagues showed modern networks are routinely miscalibrated — and softmax confidence can be arbitrarily high far outside the training distribution. The signal you'd want as a warning fails silently at exactly the boundary.

show.event: a confidence surface over the training region — high and honest inside
the surface extends BEYOND the data's edge without dipping — confidently wrong over empty space
terracotta ring on the overhang; 'Guo et al.' citation chip small

production_viz.label: high confidence, no data
production_viz.mechanic: surface overhangs the data region without dropping

beats.narration_text: So honest tooling doesn't repair the gap — nothing does; that's what constitutive means. It makes the gap LOUD. Shift detectors, widening conformal sets, out-of-distribution scores: fail loudly, not silently. Instrumentation, not reassurance. Which raises the real question: is the override real?

show.event: C3 SourceFlow: incoming cases → shift detector → alarm lane vs proceed lane
a boundary case trips the detector — the alarm fires VISIBLY and routes to a human chip
'loud, not closed' — terracotta; the gap itself stays drawn

beats.narration_text: Act five. Because every one of these limits ends at the same sentence in the deployment plan — 'a human can override' — and that sentence has a failure mode with a name.

show.event: act card 'The Override That Wasn't'

beats.narration_text: Madeleine Clare Elish named it the moral crumple zone. A car's crumple zone absorbs the crash to protect the driver. In automated systems it inverts: the structure protects the system, and the nearest human absorbs the blame — accountable for outcomes they never controlled. Law expects one person. The person crumples.

show.event: a car-frame crumples around a protected driver-mark — the mechanical version, labeled
the diagram inverts: a system-frame stays rigid; the human-operator mark at its edge deforms on impact
'the human absorbs the crash' — terracotta; 'Elish, 2019' chip small

production_viz.label: moral crumple zone
production_viz.mechanic: protective crumple inverted — rigid system, deforming human

beats.narration_text: And 'a human is watching' has been tested. Experimental work on human-in-the-loop oversight found it doesn't reliably correct algorithmic errors — and can worsen them, the overseer's own preferences shaping which errors slip through. The supervisor on the org chart can be the fictional override in the room.

show.event: error chips flow past a human-overseer gate; some pass, some caught — but the filter pattern matches the overseer's own bias chip, not the error type
'present on the chart, absent in effect' — terracotta

props.note: cited as recent experimental work; no invented percentages

beats.narration_text: The night of January twenty-seventh, nineteen eighty-six. Ice on the launch tower at Cape Canaveral. Morton Thiokol's engineers — Roger Boisjoly among them — have the O-ring cold-temperature data on the table, and they are arguing to delay the Challenger launch.
beats.new_visual_element: VOX run R2 (1/2): ice on the pad
beats.prompt: Tier 2 — NASA archival: the famous ice/icicle photos on the launch service structure, morning of STS-51-L (Jan 28, 1986). NASA imagery is public domain; sidecar required. See SHOPPING.md.

show.event: tight on icicles on the structure; slow drift
serif label: 'January 27, 1986 · the night before'

beats.narration_text: Per the Rogers Commission testimony, the sentence that ended the argument came from inside Thiokol — executive Jerry Mason to his own head of engineering, Bob Lund: take off your engineering hat, and put on your management hat. The call reconnected. Thiokol told NASA: go. Detection survived the night. Authority didn't.
beats.new_visual_element: VOX run R2 (2/2): the pad at dawn — and the sentence
beats.prompt: Tier 2 — NASA archival: wide pre-launch pad view of Challenger on 39B, dawn/frost. NO accident imagery anywhere in this reel. Sidecar required. See SHOPPING.md.

show.event: camera eases OUT from the handoff to the wide pad at dawn
the quote card lands, serif, attributed precisely: 'Mason, to Lund — Rogers Commission testimony'
'detected. not acted on.' — terracotta underline

beats.narration_text: So: an override is real only when three things hold at once. An independent limit signal — not the system's own confidence. Organizationally binding — it doesn't have to win a midnight argument. And no career cost that silence doesn't carry. Boisjoly had the first. History records what happened to the other two.

show.event: three condition rows draw with checkboxes: independent signal · binding · career-safe
the Challenger case runs the checklist: first box checks; the other two X out in sequence
'all three, or it's fiction' — terracotta

props.note: three-condition checklist; NIST/OECD alignment in SOURCES

beats.narration_text: Act six. What an honest deployment does with a limit it cannot remove.

show.event: act card 'Making the Limit Loud'

beats.narration_text: First, calibrate the humans. The gap between stated confidence and scored accuracy is expected calibration error — and it applies to the engineer signing the deployment. The forecasting fix: lock the prediction before the outcome, score it, repeat until the gap is data. Understanding calibration is not being calibrated.
beats.new_visual_element: Human ECE — the scored forecast loop

show.event: an engineer-mark states 90%; a sealed prediction card locks BEFORE the outcome arrives
outcomes land; the scored track record accumulates; the stated-vs-scored gap draws as a bar
repeat arrows loop; the gap narrows only across repetitions — terracotta on the loop

production_viz.label: lock → score → repeat
production_viz.mechanic: sealed-prediction loop narrowing a stated-vs-scored gap
production_viz.note: Good Judgment Project method; no invented percentages

beats.narration_text: Second, name the limit in the shipping documentation — model-card style, a primary artifact, not a footer disclaimer. This system is limited by: meaning, aboutness, or shift. Performance claims don't imply the limit is solved. Cases that trip the named signal route to a human with binding stop authority.

show.event: a model-card artifact draws; the NAMED STRUCTURAL LIMIT field types itself in serif
the routing line highlights: 'trips [signal] → human with binding stop/defer authority'
a greyed footer-disclaimer version X's out beside it

props.note: model cards / datasheets precedent; the template from SOURCE.md Part 7

beats.narration_text: Third — the no-deploy list, because sometimes the honest answer is no. Irreversible faster than a human can intervene. World-grounding assumed, unverifiable. Drift undetectable in time. Calibration unscoreable. An override that can't be made binding and career-safe. Any one of those — and the limit isn't a caveat. It's the verdict.

show.event: five condition chips queue at a DEPLOY gate; each triggering chip flips the gate red as it's spoken
the gate holds shut on 'the verdict' — terracotta; a small 'this is the honest achievement' subline

props.gate: any one condition → do not deploy
props.note: the source's no-deploy list, verbatim in spirit

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Symbols don't ground themselves — and a citation is not a current world. Aboutness is borrowed, on every theory that matters for deployment. The data is always less than the world, and the model's confidence fails silently exactly at the edge. An override is real only if it's independently informed, organizationally binding, and career-safe. And when those can't be made true — the limit is the verdict.

show.event: ClaudeVerdictArtifact: five bare lines land with the voice

props.title: The limit is the verdict
artifactLines: Symbols don't ground themselves; citations aren't current worlds.
Aboutness is borrowed — on every theory that matters.
The data is always less than the world; confidence fails at the edge.
A real override: independent signal, binding, career-safe.
When those can't be true, the limit is the verdict.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt: I'm evaluating a specific AI deployment. Walk the three structural limits — symbol grounding, derived intentionality, distributional shift — and tell me which one is most exposed in my context: does failure come from misreference, from pretended understanding, or from the world moving out from under the training data? Then design the documentation block that names that limit explicitly, specify what a real override requires here against the three conditions — independent signal, binding authority, no career cost — and be honest about the last question: is this a deployment where the limits, given the stakes, are a reason not to deploy at all? Run it on the system your own team is closest to shipping. Especially then.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk, greeting 'Your turn.', the full prompt typed as Liam reads it

props.command: I'm evaluating a specific AI deployment: [describe it]. (1) Walk the three structural limits — symbol grounding (meaning), derived intentionality (aboutness), and distributional shift (the data-world gap) — and identify which is most exposed here: misreference, pretended understanding, or a moving world. (2) Design a documentation section that names that limit explicitly, model-card style, not as a footer disclaimer. (3) Specify what a REAL override requires in this context, checked against three conditions: an independent limit signal (not the system's own confidence), organizationally binding authority, and no asymmetric career cost for using it. (4) Answer honestly: is this a deployment where the limits, given the stakes, are a reason not to deploy at all?

beats.narration_text: What the Tools Cannot Do. Liam, in for Bear.

show.event: ClaudeTitleOutro: poster serif title, terracotta period, handle
